_about: The CPL Initiative governance register — a STARTER draft (SkyMail, Session 120, 2026-08-05) written at Sam's request after a session where every problem hit turned out to be a governance gap wearing a data-quality costume. Rendered by governance.js as the team-gated Governance tab. This file is the REASONING + the allocations; anything that can be MEASURED is computed live at render time instead of stored here, so the tab cannot quietly disagree with reality (the pattern from methodology-register-is-the-spine-narrative-cites-it).
_status: DRAFT — for review by Sam, Ashley, Jessica, Malone. Every `owner` field is deliberately null: who is accountable on OUR side is the one thing a session cannot infer from data. Filling those in is the review.
_principle: Colleges are locally governed. We route to determinations they already made; we do not make determinations for them. Where the CO does hold authority, say so explicitly — ambiguity produces both over-reach and paralysis.

decision_rights.drives: MAP routes a student's CPL request to this address. Empty = the request reaches nobody.
decision_rights.maintained_in: MAP platform (no write API — only the college can set it)
decision_rights.when_empty: We propose someone the college already designated in MAP and tell them we did. We never appoint.
Eligibility badge is absent. No substitute is invented.

decision_rights.drives: Discipline inference, CTE flag, the CIP crosswalk.
decision_rights.decides: College faculty at local curriculum approval
decision_rights.when_empty: Nothing downstream may gate on it. See AS-03 — this is our most developed acceptance standard and the template for the rest.

decision_rights.drives: The whole unified-course layer and the eventual C-ID submission pathway.
decision_rights.decides: CPL Initiative (CO) — explicitly AI-assisted STAGING, not faculty-published
decision_rights.when_empty: Re-mints permitted under the playbook. Rule re-locks to 'stable identifiers' once we declare the layer faculty-published — that declaration is itself a governance act with no owner today.
Never re-keyed, never invented. We submit; they decide.

decision_rights.element: Articulated exhibits (what a college grants credit for)
decision_rights.drives: Every CPL award a student actually receives.
decision_rights.when_empty: The gap is an outreach worklist, not a build backlog.

decision_rights.drives: How exhibits collapse into one credential across colleges.
decision_rights.when_empty: Falls back to the college's freehand title, which is why the canonicalization exists.

decision_rights.drives: Where a student actually lands, and where our nudges deep-link.
decision_rights.when_empty: 3 of 123 have none. A college with no page cannot receive a routed request at all.
n/a — this is ours to set, and the one place on this list where WE are the authority rather than a router.

decision_rights.element: Who a college's MAP users are
decision_rights.drives: Access to MAP; who can act on CPL at that college.
decision_rights.when_empty: 3 institutions have ZERO active users. That is an onboarding problem, not a contact problem — do not paper over it with a routing fix.

decision_rights.element: What Sierra tells the public (answer rules + guardrails)
decision_rights.drives: Sierra is embedded on colleges' own pages and answers students, prospective students, faculty, administrators and employers. Her rule text IS the product — it decides what a CPL seeker is told exists, and how a host college is characterised on its own site.
decision_rights.decides: CPL Initiative (CO) — in practice Sam personally, four consecutive times on 2026-08-06/07 (either/or → Yes/And → the portal's fuller portfolio → anti-poaching → the salesmanship/facts tie-break)
decision_rights.when_empty: Each rule change gets resolved ad hoc by whichever session is running. Two consequences already observed: (1) a rule written purely as a prohibition made Sierra WITHHOLD facts from seekers, and nothing caught it because the prohibition was the only half tested; (2) two rules in different constants conflicted with nothing saying which governed, so the later one silently won. Also unowned: prompt text only takes effect ON DEPLOY, so 'decided' and 'live' are distinct states and no one tracks the gap between them.

acceptance_standards.rule: The system of record for what a college has articulated. We surface it; we never edit it (no write API by design — see the surface-don't-edit ADR).

Authoritative for WHO the college named, but the values are not validated at entry: 15 colleges hold several addresses in one cell and some hold single-character junk. Parse, never trust as a single clean value.

Faculty-entered with no data-entry gatekeeper. NEVER gates a determination (discipline / identity / membership / merge). Usable only when a second independent signal agrees. Authoritative in exactly two places: the CTE flag and the CIP↔TOP crosswalk. This is the most developed standard we have — use it as the template for every new input.
Same posture as TOP: corroborate, don't gate, until it demonstrates reliability. Decide the promotion criteria BEFORE the cutover, not after we're depending on it.
Reliable that a course/program exists; lags on currency, and the program-course membership file is partially populated — treat joins through it as a LOWER BOUND.
Record who said it and when, so it stays questionable later rather than only believable-or-deletable. A curator MAY name an individual where a lookup may not — they know who actually answers.
A starting point to verify, never a designation. Show the source link. Department inboxes only — naming an individual from a web page is a determination we don't have standing to make.
Anything I derive is a proposal until a human or a second independent signal confirms it. Where I've guessed, the artifact should say so — that is what the provenance tiers are for.

cadences.note: The instrument was built in June and has never been fired. A cadence nobody runs is a document, not governance. This is the single most actionable item on this page.
Deliberately manual: a human-reviewed draft PR IS the sensitivity audit. Correct as designed; it just has no named reviewer.

The same shape as CA-03, but a step worse: that loop was decided and never fired; this one was never even decided. Measured 2026-08-07 — of 56 ratings since 1 July, not one had ever moved off status='new'. 31 of them are our own CI smoke test, which writes through the public anon RPC on every run and CANNOT delete its own rows (anon is deliberately write-only on that table). That share is visibly growing: it went 28 -> 31 during a single working session, purely from re-running the test. The unread rows were not noise — a geography bug reported 2026-07-03 sat five weeks, and a student-routing report on 2026-07-17 described a problem only fixed three weeks later, after it happened to come up in conversation. 4 rows have now been marked addressed; 7 real thumbs-down remain. GATE: the MAP/CO test invitation should not go out until this has an owner — inviting people into a channel nobody reads manufactures unread rows and teaches the team their feedback goes nowhere.

open_questions.why: Every `owner` is null. A decision right with no accountable person is a description of the past, not governance. This is the review.

open_questions.q: Is there an existing MOU or participation agreement with colleges that already allocates some of these rights?
open_questions.why: If so, this register should MIRROR it rather than invent a parallel structure. I can't see those documents.

open_questions.q: What are the promotion criteria for CIP — what would it have to demonstrate to move from advisory to corroborating to authoritative?
open_questions.why: Fall 2026 cutover. Decide before we depend on it; TOP shows what happens when an input is trusted by default.
The rules change materially at that moment (re-mints stop). Today no one owns making that call or knows what evidence it requires.
I marked 8 of 10 as load-bearing from the data's behavior, which is almost certainly too many. Governing everything is how governance dies — cut this list.

open_questions.q: Should this tab be team-gated or public?
open_questions.why: Gated today. A public decision-rights table could be genuinely good for college trust — but 'last run: never' is a bad look before it's addressed. Fix the cadence first, then consider opening it.

open_questions.q: What has to be true before we invite the MAP and CO teams to test Sierra?
open_questions.why: Sam wants to open Sierra up to the wider team. The invitation is cheap; the failure is not. At minimum it needs CA-06 to have a named owner and a stated frequency, and DR-11 to have someone who decides when a reported behaviour is a bug versus a product choice — the last four rule changes were all the latter, and all of them needed Sam. Worth deciding whether the invitation is staged (MAP team first, CO second) so the queue's volume is survivable while the loop is new.
